$note: BroGram lessons. One lesson per CLO. No institution names, no pattern ids, no emoji.

lessons.title: Tags Carry Meaning
lessons.hook: A missing alt attribute turns a real photo into silence for a screen reader.

blocks.heading: The Tree Under the Page
blocks.body: Every tag becomes a node in two trees: the one the browser paints, and the accessibility tree that screen readers read instead of pixels. A plain `div` says nothing about what it holds; a `button` or `nav` announces its own job by name. Images carry no words at all unless you give them one: the `alt` attribute is the sentence a screen reader speaks in place of the picture. Skip it on a photo that matters and it becomes empty space. A purely decorative image gets `alt=""` so it is skipped on purpose, not by accident. Reading a tag's own attributes back in script is a quick way to check what actually shipped, not what you meant to write.

steps.say: Empty alt is a deliberate signal: skip this image, it carries no extra meaning.
A real alt survives even if the image never loads, so the data is not lost.
Grabbing both elements first keeps the comparison honest instead of guessing.
Printing `.alt.length` proves what actually reached the accessibility tree.

blocks.caption: Two images, two different reasons for their alt text.

blocks.prompt: say(id) is true only when the alt is a real description. The star is decorative, the thumbnail's alt was copied from the file name, and the map has a written sentence. What does this print?
blocks.hint: Run say in your head on each image: does it have words, and are those words anything more than the file name?
blocks.explain: thumb has words, but they are the file name, so the second test fails it. star is empty on purpose, so the first test fails it. Only map carries a sentence a screen reader can actually use.

blocks.prompt:
This page has one image, `#hero`, whose `alt` is still empty even though the photo is not decorative -- it is the page's main team photo.

Write a script that sets `#hero`'s `alt` to a real description of the photo, a few actual words, not the filename.

Example: alt could read something like "Three teammates high-fiving at a launch party".

tests.input: const alt = document.getElementById('hero').alt; return (alt && alt.trim().length > 5) ? 'ok' : 'alt is still empty or too short'
tests.name: alt is filled in

tests.input: const alt = document.getElementById('hero').alt.toLowerCase(); return alt.includes('team.jpg') ? 'alt still looks like a filename' : 'ok'
tests.name: not just the filename

blocks.hint: Set the element's alt property to a plain-language description, not the filename.
blocks.explain: Assigning alt describes the photo for anyone who cannot see it; an empty string said "nothing here," which was false since this image matters.

bullets: Tag names build the tree screen readers actually read.
Empty alt means decorative on purpose, not by accident.
A missing or filename-only alt turns real content into silence.
blocks.remember: If a screen reader cannot say it, the page has not really said it either.

blocks.say: Time to hunt real markup where alt text is missing, wrong, or just a filename.

lessons.exitLine: Time to hunt real markup where alt text is missing, wrong, or just a filename.

lessons.title: Where The Leftover Space Goes
lessons.hook: Flexbox lines things up in one move. The real skill is deciding where the leftover room goes.

blocks.heading: justify-content decides where the leftover space lands
blocks.body: Give a container display: flex and its direct children line up in a row by default, side by side instead of stacking. justify-content then decides what happens to whatever width is left over once the children are sized. flex-start pushes everything left, leaving the extra room after the last item. center bunches the children together and splits the extra room evenly before the first and after the last. space-between spreads the children across the full width so the first sits at the left edge, the last sits at the right edge, and the extra room becomes equal gaps only between the ones in the middle. Pick the value by where the leftover space should land.

blocks.code: Home Docs About

steps.say: display: flex turns nav into a row container, so the three links sit side by side.
space-between hands the leftover width to the gaps between links, not to the links themselves.
Only nav's direct children, the three links, become flex items here; nothing nested deeper counts.
Home pins to the left edge and About to the right; the two gaps between them grow equally.

blocks.caption: One row, three links, the leftover width absorbed by the gaps between them.

blocks.prompt: Same nav, but justify-content is changed to center instead of space-between. Where does the leftover width go now?
options: Split into two equal margins, one before the first link and one after the last, with the links bunched together in the middle
Spread evenly only between the links, with nothing before the first or after the last
Added entirely after the last link, so the links pack against the left edge
why: Right. center treats the whole leftover width as two matching margins around the bunched-together group.
That description fits space-between, not center — center does not touch the space between individual links.
That fits flex-start, not center — center never leaves the group pressed against one edge.
blocks.hint: center is about grouping the children, not spacing them apart. Where would two matching margins have to sit?
blocks.explain: center treats the three links as one tight group and puts all of the leftover width into two equal margins, one before the group and one after it, so nothing opens up between the links themselves.

blocks.prompt: The three buttons should spread across the toolbar with space-between, but they sit bunched together at the left edge instead. Which line breaks it?
blocks.hint: Check the value given to display on that line — is that a real CSS keyword?
blocks.explain: display: flexbox is not a valid value; the keyword is flex. The browser drops that whole declaration, .toolbar never becomes a flex container, and justify-content has no row left to act on.

blocks.prompt: Fill in the two missing declarations in .toolbar so the three buttons form a flex row with the leftover width spread out as equal gaps between them, none before the first and none after the last.

tests.name: container is a flex row
leftover space goes between items

blocks.hint: One property turns the container into a flex row. Another says how the leftover width should be shared.
blocks.explain: display: flex turns .toolbar into a flex row, and justify-content: space-between sends every pixel of leftover width into the gaps between buttons, leaving none before the first or after the last.

bullets: display: flex turns direct children into a row by default.
justify-content decides where leftover width goes, not item order.
space-between fills only the middle gaps; the edges stay pinned.
blocks.remember: justify-content controls the leftover space, not the items themselves.

blocks.say: Next you write that rule yourself, on a layout you have not seen yet.

lessons.exitLine: That's the leftover-space rule. Time to write it into a layout of your own.

lessons.title: Stop the submit, then check it
lessons.hook: preventDefault() is the one line standing between you and a page that reloads before you can check anything.

blocks.heading: Events let your code react before the page moves on
blocks.body: A page can react to what someone does — a click, a key press, a form submit — by listening for that action with addEventListener. Give it an event name and a function, and the browser calls your function the instant that action happens. A form's submit event normally reloads the page immediately, before you get a say. Call event.preventDefault() as the very first line of your handler and that reload never happens, so you get to look at what was typed first. Read a field's value, test it against a rule, and if it fails, write your own message onto the page and stop. If it passes, let the rest of your code run.

blocks.caption: Change the value so it has no @ and run it again. Watch which line logs.

steps.say: Listening for submit means your code runs the instant the button fires it.
preventDefault stops the page reload, so your checks get to run before anything is sent.
Trimming catches spaces-only input, and returning early stops a bad value from going any further.
Clearing the old error first stops a stale message lingering after a fix.

blocks.caption: One field, checked before it ever leaves the page.

blocks.prompt: Same shape, a different form. What does this log when the button fires?
blocks.hint: Trace what qty becomes once the text '0' is turned into a number.
blocks.explain: Number('0') is 0, and 0 is not greater than 0, so the guard catches it and logs the rejection message instead of ever reaching the order line.

blocks.prompt: You delete event.preventDefault() from the handler above. The name field is empty and the button is clicked. What happens?
options: Nothing changes — the check still stops the page from submitting.
The browser reloads the page as soon as submit fires, before the error message can be seen.
The error message shows twice instead of once.
why: The check still runs and still writes the message, but nothing stops the browser's normal reload from happening right after.
Right. preventDefault is the only thing stopping the reload. Skip it, and the page reloads regardless of what the check decided.
The handler still only runs once per click, so nothing here would make a message double up.
blocks.hint: Think about what preventDefault is actually stopping the browser from doing.
blocks.explain: preventDefault is the only thing standing between your check and the browser's default reload. Remove it and the reload happens no matter what the check found, so the message never gets a chance to be read.

blocks.prompt: Finish the handler: an empty comment should set the status to 'Write something first.' and stop there; anything else should set it to 'Posted.'

tests.name: empty comment
real comment
recovers after an empty submit

blocks.hint: Guard first: check the length, set the message, and return before anything else runs.
blocks.explain: An empty comment needs to stop immediately with its own message so nothing posts; anything else should fall through to the success line.

bullets: addEventListener runs your code the moment an event happens.
preventDefault stops the reload so your check runs first.
Guard bad input early, then let good input through.
blocks.remember: Check before you let it go — the page never gets a free pass.

blocks.say: Different form, real input. Time to write the check yourself.

lessons.exitLine: That's the guard. Now go build one that has to hold up.

lessons.title: One signal, three layers
lessons.hook: One flipped attribute, and the whole page reacts — layout, text, everything.

blocks.heading: One flipped signal, three layers in sync
blocks.body: When a page needs to look different depending on what a person just did, resist wiring HTML, CSS, and JavaScript separately and hoping they stay in sync. Instead, pick one small signal — a class name, or a data attribute's value — that JavaScript flips on an interaction, and let the CSS rules key off that same signal. The markup only needs to declare the piece that can change. The script only needs to flip one thing. The stylesheet only needs to read it, and nothing else has to be told. If a menu is open, a form step is done, or a card is expanded, one flipped signal drives every visual change at once.

blocks.caption: Click the button. Only the attribute flips — the CSS rule is what does the rest.

blocks.code:
Water the plants

Every morning before class, five minutes.

steps.say: The markup only holds the one piece that changes: an attribute, and a hidden paragraph.
CSS reads that same attribute value, so there is no separate class logic to keep synced.
One click reads the current state and flips it — the single fact everything else depends on.
Revealing the paragraph and relabeling the button both fall out of that one flipped value.

blocks.caption: One attribute, read by CSS and flipped by JavaScript, drives the whole card.

blocks.prompt: Same idea, a light/dark switch instead of a details card. The button is clicked three times before anything prints. What prints?
blocks.hint: Trace three flips starting from light. An odd number of flips never lands back where it started.
blocks.explain: Each click flips data-theme once: light to dark, dark to light, light to dark. Three clicks is an odd number of flips, so it ends on dark, the opposite of where it began.

blocks.prompt: The section starts hidden and the button starts labeled "Show". Finish the script so one click reveals the section and relabels the button, and a second click reverses both — using the data-open attribute the CSS already watches.
blocks.starterCode: More detail lives here.

tests.input: document.querySelector('#expand').click(); const p = document.querySelector('#panel'); const b = document.querySelector('#expand'); return (p.dataset.open === 'true' && b.textContent === 'Hide') ? 'ok' : 'did not open';
tests.name: one click opens

tests.input: const b = document.querySelector('#expand'); b.click(); b.click(); const p = document.querySelector('#panel'); return (p.dataset.open === 'false' && b.textContent === 'Show') ? 'ok' : 'did not close again';
tests.name: second click closes

blocks.referenceSolution: More detail lives here.
blocks.hint: Read panel.dataset.open first, decide the opposite value, then set the attribute and the button text from that one decision.
blocks.explain: Reading dataset.open before changing it lets one flipped value drive both the attribute CSS watches and the button's label, so the two never disagree.

bullets: Pick one small attribute or class as the single source of truth.
CSS reads that same value — nothing to keep in sync by hand.
One click flips it once, and every visual change follows from that.
blocks.remember: One flipped signal can drive layout, text, and behaviour together.

blocks.say: Time to wire a whole page yourself — structure, style, and one signal between them.

lessons.exitLine: That's the wiring. Now go build a page that holds together on its own.
